content: 1. Reliable supply chains for test kits and treatments are essential to ensure consistent implementation and monitoring of syphilis screening and treatment programs (Ansbro, 2015). 2. The quality of care has been shown to improve with enhanced supply chain management and better supervision of healthcare workers (Nnko, 2015). 3. Syphilis identification and treatment can be improved without compromising HIV services, and it is feasible to conduct multiple rapid tests simultaneously (Strasser, 2012). 4. Laboratory staff support is necessary for nurses and midwives to effectively administer point-of-care tests (Mabey, 2015). 5. Increased testing and treatment rates can be achieved by integrating point-of-care tests (POCTs) into existing healthcare systems (Mabey, 2012). 6. Policymakers and public health officials should be involved from the outset when integrating POCTs into healthcare systems (Mabey, 2012). 7. The high per-unit cost of rapid syphilis tests (RSTs) has made them unaffordable for some programs (Kleutsch, 2009). 8. Adequate donor contributions to national health spending are necessary to support syphilis screening and treatment programs (Kleutsch, 2009). 9. Decentralized screening interventions, including on-site and off-site rapid plasma reagin (RPR) testing and treatment, have increased testing uptake, treatment rates, and reduced adverse pregnancy outcomes such as perinatal death and stillbirth in lowand middle-income countries (Hawkes, 2011). 10. Syphilis screening using RSTs has been successfully implemented in diverse settings, ranging from urban areas in China and Peru to remote villages in East Africa and indigenous populations in the Amazon rainforest (Mabey, 2012). 11. The introduction of POCTs has increased syphilis screening coverage to over 90% in countries such as Brazil, China, Peru, Uganda, Tanzania, and Zambia, compared to traditional RPR testing (Mabey, 2012). 12. Barriers such as transportation costs for collecting laboratory results, geographical distance from healthcare facilities, and long waiting times can be mitigated by the availability of rapid tests, which improve accessibility (Ansbro, 2015). 13. A slight increase in partner testing rates was observed when general invitation letters were sent to partners of antenatal care attendees, and targeted letters were sent to partners of syphilis-positive women (Strasser, 2012). 14. Training and quality assurance are critical components when implementing rapid syphilis tests, as agreed upon by the Guideline Development Group (GDG). 15. The WHO guidelines recommend on-site rapid syphilis tests (RSTs) in settings with low syphilis screening coverage, high loss to follow-up, or limited laboratory capacity, rather than standard off-site laboratory-based screening and treatment strategies (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). 16. In settings with low syphilis prevalence (below 5%), the WHO suggests using a single on-site RST for screening pregnant women rather than a single on-site RPR test (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). 17. In high-prevalence settings (5% or greater), the WHO recommends a sequence of on-site RST followed by treatment if positive, an RPR test, and further treatment based on syphilis duration if the RPR test is also positive (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). 18. These recommendations do not apply to countries with the capacity to provide high-quality laboratory-based screening and treatment strategies. However, in resource-limited settings, a single on-site RST may be suggested to ensure greater screening coverage, despite the risk of over-treatment due to false-positive results. 19. The use of a single on-site RST followed by treatment (Strategy A) or an on-site RST followed by an RPR test and additional treatment if positive (Strategy C) may result in slightly to moderately higher treatment rates compared to on-site RPR strategies (Strategies B and C) across all prevalence settings. 20. The difference in harms caused by over-treatment is minimal between single on-site RST (Strategy A) and single on-site RPR test (Strategy B) in low-prevalence settings but may be moderate in high-prevalence settings, favoring the RST strategy. 21. The number of pregnant women screened appears to be slightly higher or similar with the single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) compared to other strategies, regardless of prevalence settings. 22. The GDG emphasized the importance of prioritizing missed syphilis cases due to the severe adverse effects of syphilis in pregnancy, including congenital syphilis and fetal death. 23. Over-treatment, while associated with minor side effects such as gastrointestinal symptoms, was considered acceptable in some cases but undesirable when occurring in large proportions of tested women. 24. Although there is no direct evidence on the impact of different strategies on partner notification, the GDG agreed that a sequence of tests (Strategy C) could increase partner treatment by enhancing confidence in positive results among tested women and their partners. 25. Cost-effectiveness modeling indicates that the total costs per 1,000 women screened are lowest with RPR in some settings (e.g., Tanzania and Zambia) but lowest with RSTs in others (e.g., Peru) due to labor costs associated with RPR. 26. The most cost-effective approach across all prevalence settings is a single on-site RST followed by treatment if positive (Strategy A), though costs may vary in different settings. 27. On-site RSTs have been successfully implemented in many countries, demonstrating feasibility and acceptability among healthcare workers and pregnant women. 28. Healthcare providers should receive training and information about syphilis prevalence in pregnant women and the risks of mother-to-child transmission. 29. Pregnant women and their partners may require additional support when discussing partner treatment. 30. Research priorities include trials comparing the sensitivity and specificity of test sequences, as well as studies assessing outcomes such as partner notification, treatment, and long-term consequences for mothers and infants.
